newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Cotton seen falling in Pakistan, rising in India.
newsitem.headline: Cotton seen falling in Pakistan, rising in India.

text.p: Cotton prices are likely to fall on low demand in Pakistan and rise in India on transporters strike short term, dealers said on Friday.
In Pakistan unsold stocks total about 1.4 million 375-lb bales due to low demand from textile mills and low exports due to high prices in the domestic markets, dealer Kishin Chand said.
Shortage of funds added to the bearish sentiment in the market, Chand said.

Pakistan's customs-cleared cotton exports fell to 33,387 bales between September 1, 1996 and April 4, compared to 1.706 million in the same period a year-ago, an official of the private Karachi Cotton Association (KCA) said.
Rates fluctuated slightly in the kerb market where mills buying on cash purchased at a lower price than the prevailing official rates at the KCA, one dealer said.
In the kerb market, NIAB-78 variety was quoted 2,050/2,100 rupees per maund (37.32 kg), K-68 2,400/2,450 and MNH-93 2,425/2,475, the dealer said.
Prices are likely to fall in the next few days as ginners, who were holding 1.446 million bales of unsold stocks last month, plan to unload the stocks on to the market, the dealer said.

In India, an indefinite strike by truck operators has crippled the movement of cotton, affecting its supply and pushing up prices, traders said.
The transporters, who pulled their trucks off the road from Tuesday, are demanding the withdrawal of a five percent service charge and scrapping of a proposed rise in insurance premiums.
"Cotton yarn and textile mills are complaining about the shortage of ready stock while farmers are facing inventory problems," said a trader.
In the week to Thursday, cotton prices recovered on reduced arrivals despite sluggish demand from mills.

In spot, Bengal-deshi rose 20/30 rupees to 900/940 rupees per maund (37.32 kg) and Punjab saw-ginned 10/60 rupees to 1,560/1,660 rupees per maund. F-414 gained 10/50 rupees to 1,890/1,950 rupees per maund.
Gujarat Kalyan (medium-staple) rose 300/500 rupees to 13,500/13,800 rupees per candy (355.56 kg).
"Arrivals have also dropped as most of the current season crop has been marketed," said Chandulal Thakkar, a leading cotton dealer.
He said nearly 14.50 million bales of cotton (one bale is 170 kg) out of an estimated crop of 16 million bales in the 1996/97 (October/September) had been sold.
"I'm expecting a further drop in arrivals in the coming weeks," Thakkar said.
Traders said the government's recent decision to allow an additional export of 20 million kg of cotton yarn had also cheered market sentiment.
"So far mill demand has been low but now I expect improved buying of cotton by spinning mills," Thakkar said.
($1 = 40.22 Pakistani rupees)
